Teaching points: Regular vs irregular rhythm (monomorphic usually regular, polymorphic may be irregular), baseline QT interval on previous ECG (crucial for diagnosis), patient haemodynamic status (dictates urgency of intervention). Safety: Both require continuous monitoring, IV access, defibrillator at bedside, senior cardiology input for definitive management decisions.
mcqs.summary: Monomorphic VT (uniform QRS) suggests stable re-entrant circuit from scar tissue; polymorphic VT (varying QRS) suggests unstable substrate from acute ischaemia, QT prolongation, or electrolyte disturbance. Morphology guides treatment.

question.scenario: A 28-year-old male medical student presents to the GP clinic after detecting irregular heartbeats while measuring his own pulse during a physiology practical. He reports occasional 'skipped beats' for the past 6 months, occurring 2-3 times per week, lasting a few seconds, not associated with chest pain, dyspnoea, syncope or presyncope. He exercises regularly (runs 5 km three times weekly) without symptoms. There is no family history of sudden cardiac death or cardiomyopathy. Physical examination: HR 68 bpm with occasional irregular beats, BP 118/72 mmHg, cardiovascular examination otherwise normal. 12-lead ECG shows sinus rhythm with frequent isolated premature ventricular complexes (PVCs), 6 per minute, unifocal morphology, no couplets or runs of VT. Echocardiography: structurally normal heart, LVEF 62%, no valvular abnormalities.
question.stem: What is the most appropriate management approach for this patient?

options.A: Reassure that these are benign ventricular ectopics, advise reduction in caffeine intake and avoidance of excessive alcohol, no specific treatment required, arrange follow-up only if symptoms become troublesome
options.B: Commence beta-blocker therapy (metoprolol 25 mg daily) to suppress ventricular ectopics and reduce risk of progression to ventricular tachycardia
options.C: Refer urgently to cardiology for 24-hour Holter monitoring and exercise stress testing to exclude underlying cardiomyopathy or channelopathy
options.D: Arrange cardiac MRI to exclude arrhythmogenic right ventricular cardiomyopathy (ARVC) and genetic testing for Brugada syndrome

mcqs.explanation: This patient has benign ventricular ectopic beats (also called premature ventricular complexes or PVCs) in the context of a structurally normal heart, which requires reassurance rather than intervention. Key features supporting benign nature: (1) Young patient with no cardiovascular symptoms (no syncope, chest pain, dyspnoea, palpitations beyond awareness of ectopics); (2) No family history of sudden cardiac death or inherited cardiac conditions; (3) Structurally normal heart on echocardiography with normal left ventricular function (LVEF 62%); (4) Unifocal PVCs (single morphology suggests single benign focus) with relatively low frequency (6/minute = ~8,000-10,000 per 24 hours, which is <10% of total beats); (5) No couplets, triplets or runs of non-sustained VT; (6) Good exercise tolerance. In this context, ventricular ectopics are extremely common in healthy individuals - up to 50% of healthy adults have occasional PVCs on 24-hour monitoring, and they increase with age. They are usually triggered by stimulants (caffeine, nicotine, alcohol, sympathomimetic drugs), stress, fatigue or electrolyte disturbances. Management involves: (1) Reassurance that these are not dangerous and do not require treatment; (2) Lifestyle modification - reduce caffeine (coffee, energy drinks, pre-workout supplements common in medical students), avoid excessive alcohol, ensure adequate sleep and stress management; (3) Review medications (no sympathomimetics, bronchodilators, decongestants); (4) Follow-up only if symptoms become more frequent or troublesome, or if new symptoms develop (syncope, presyncope, chest pain). No pharmacological treatment is indicated as PVCs in structurally normal hearts do not increase mortality risk. Option B (beta-blocker therapy) is not routinely recommended for benign PVCs. While beta-blockers can suppress ectopics, they are reserved for patients with frequent symptomatic PVCs causing significant quality of life impairment despite lifestyle modification, or very high PVC burden (>15-20% of beats) risking PVC-induced cardiomyopathy. This patient does not meet these criteria. Option C (urgent cardiology referral) is unnecessarily aggressive. While Holter monitoring and stress testing can be considered if there are concerning features (syncope, family history of sudden death, symptoms during exercise, frequent or complex ectopics), this patient has already had structural assessment (echocardiography) which is normal. Cardiology referral would be indicated if: (1) Symptoms during exercise; (2) Frequent polymorphic PVCs or runs of NSVT; (3) Declining LV function; (4) PVC burden >15%; (5) Family history of sudden death. Option D (cardiac MRI and genetic testing) is also excessive. ARVC typically presents with exercise-induced symptoms, polymorphic or LBBB-morphology VT, and structural RV changes. Brugada syndrome shows characteristic ECG pattern (RBBB with ST elevation in V1-V3) and presents with syncope or sudden death. Neither is suggested by this presentation. Differential diagnoses to exclude: (1) Frequent PVCs with high burden (>15%) - risk of PVC-induced cardiomyopathy, requires Holter monitoring; (2) PVCs triggered by structural heart disease - echocardiography already normal; (3) PVCs in context of channelopathy (long QT, Brugada, CPVT) - would have ECG changes, family history or syncope; (4) Atrial ectopics - may feel similar to patient but have different ECG morphology. Red flags that would change management: Syncope or presyncope, PVCs increasing during exercise (suggests ARVC or CPVT), family history of sudden death <40 years, abnormal echocardiography, very frequent PVCs on Holter (>20,000/24 hours). Safety netting: Advise patient to represent if develops syncope, chest pain, dyspnoea, or if ectopics become significantly more frequent or symptomatic.
mcqs.summary: Benign ventricular ectopics in structurally normal hearts require reassurance and lifestyle modification (reduce caffeine/alcohol) only. No treatment needed unless very frequent (>15% burden) or causing significant symptoms despite lifestyle changes.

question.scenario: A 56-year-old man is admitted to the intensive care unit following successful resuscitation from an out-of-hospital cardiac arrest. Paramedics found him in ventricular fibrillation and delivered three shocks before return of spontaneous circulation (ROSC). He has a history of anterior myocardial infarction 2 years ago (PCI to LAD at that time) with residual LVEF of 35% on echocardiography performed 3 months ago. Post-resuscitation ECG shows Q waves in V1-V4 (old anterior MI) with no acute ST changes. Troponin is mildly elevated (consistent with cardiac arrest, not acute MI). Coronary angiography shows patent LAD stent with no new culprit lesion. Neurological examination shows GCS 15 post-targeted temperature management. He is extubated on day 3 and makes full neurological recovery.
question.stem: According to Australian and international guidelines, what is the most appropriate long-term management to reduce risk of further sudden cardiac death in this patient?

options.A: Implantable cardioverter-defibrillator (ICD) implantation for secondary prevention, as he has survived cardiac arrest due to VF/VT in the absence of a reversible cause
options.B: Amiodarone 200 mg daily for life, as medical management is equally effective as ICD and avoids device complications
options.C: Wearable cardioverter-defibrillator (LifeVest) for 3 months, then reassess LVEF; only implant ICD if LVEF remains <35%
options.D: Reassurance and optimisation of heart failure medications only, as the VF was triggered by acute ischaemia during the arrest and is now resolved

mcqs.explanation: This patient has a clear indication for implantable cardioverter-defibrillator (ICD) insertion for secondary prevention of sudden cardiac death (SCD). He has survived a cardiac arrest due to ventricular fibrillation in the absence of a reversible cause (angiography showed no acute culprit lesion, troponin elevation was due to arrest itself not new MI). This meets criteria for secondary prevention ICD implantation per Australian and international guidelines (AHA/ACC/HRS, ESC). ICD therapy in secondary prevention reduces mortality by approximately 50% compared to medical therapy alone - landmark trials (AVID, CIDS, CASH) demonstrated superiority of ICD over amiodarone in survivors of VF/VT arrest. The mechanism of benefit is immediate termination of VF/VT via defibrillation or anti-tachycardia pacing before haemodynamic collapse occurs. This patient has additional risk factors for recurrent VT/VF: (1) Severe LV dysfunction (LVEF 35%, normal >55%) - reduces ejection fraction increases risk of ventricular arrhythmias due to electrical instability; (2) Structural heart disease (old anterior MI with scar tissue) - creates substrate for re-entrant ventricular arrhythmias; (3) Proven susceptibility to VF (arrested once, high risk of recurrence). Timing of ICD implantation: Should occur before discharge from hospital (typically 5-7 days post-arrest once neurologically stable). Delay is only warranted if: (1) Awaiting medication optimisation in newly diagnosed heart failure; (2) Ischaemia-mediated VF within 48 hours of acute MI (wait 40 days post-MI to reassess LVEF); (3) Uncertainty about neurological prognosis. This patient has made full neurological recovery and has chronic LV dysfunction (not acute), so ICD should proceed promptly. Option B (amiodarone alone) is inferior to ICD for secondary prevention. While amiodarone reduces arrhythmia frequency, it does not prevent sudden death as effectively as ICD - AVID trial showed ICD reduced mortality by 31% vs amiodarone at 3 years. Amiodarone is typically used as adjunct to ICD in patients with recurrent ICD shocks despite optimal programming. Option C (wearable cardioverter-defibrillator/WCD) is used for temporary protection in specific scenarios: (1) Newly diagnosed heart failure awaiting LVEF reassessment at 3 months post-optimisation of medical therapy (primary prevention); (2) Bridge to ICD in patients with temporary contraindication (infection, awaiting surgery); (3) High-risk patients awaiting transplant. This patient needs definitive secondary prevention ICD, not temporary WCD. Option D (reassurance only) is incorrect as there is no reversible cause identified - angiography showed no new lesion, and VF occurred in context of chronic scar-mediated substrate, not acute ischaemia. Additional management considerations: (1) Optimise heart failure medical therapy (ACE inhibitor/ARB, beta-blocker, mineralocorticoid receptor antagonist, SGLT2 inhibitor) to improve LVEF and reduce arrhythmia burden; (2) Consider cardiac resynchronisation therapy (CRT) if QRS >150 ms and LBBB morphology - combined CRT-D device may be appropriate; (3) Assess for need for adjunct amiodarone if recurrent VT/VF episodes post-ICD; (4) VT ablation if recurrent ICD shocks despite medical therapy; (5) Genetic counselling and family screening if suspicion of inherited channelopathy (not suggested by this case). Differential diagnosis of cardiac arrest: (1) Acute MI - excluded by angiography; (2) Inherited arrhythmia syndrome (Brugada, long QT, CPVT) - unlikely given age and structural heart disease; (3) Electrolyte disturbance - should be checked and corrected; (4) Drug-induced (cocaine, QT-prolonging medications) - excluded by history. Safety considerations: ICD complications include lead dislodgement, infection, inappropriate shocks (10-15% over 3 years), device malfunction. Patients require lifelong device surveillance (every 3-6 months) and driving restrictions (private vehicle 6 months post-implant if no shocks, commercial vehicle permanently restricted in Australia). Psychological support important as many patients develop anxiety about shocks. Teaching hospital context: Cardiology/electrophysiology input required for device selection and programming, multidisciplinary team involvement (heart failure nurses, physiotherapist, psychologist), patient education about device function and restrictions.
mcqs.summary: Cardiac arrest survivor with VF in absence of reversible cause requires ICD for secondary prevention. ICD reduces mortality by 50% vs medical therapy alone. Implant before discharge once neurologically stable.

question.scenario: A 32-year-old man presents to the emergency department with syncope. He collapsed suddenly while walking to his car after work, with brief loss of consciousness for approximately 30 seconds. He reports two previous similar episodes in his twenties. His brother died suddenly aged 28 during sleep (cause unknown). He is currently asymptomatic with normal vital signs (BP 128/76 mmHg, HR 72 bpm, GCS 15). ECG shows sinus rhythm with a coved-type ST-segment elevation of 2-3 mm in leads V1-V2, followed by a negative T wave. The QRS duration is 110 ms with a partial right bundle branch block pattern. Echocardiography shows structurally normal heart with LVEF 60%.
question.stem: Based on the likely diagnosis, which of the following medication classes should be strictly avoided in this patient due to risk of provoking fatal arrhythmias?

options.A: Class Ic antiarrhythmic drugs (flecainide, propafenone) and other sodium channel blockers, as these can unmask or worsen the ECG phenotype and precipitate ventricular fibrillation in Brugada syndrome
options.B: Beta-blockers (metoprolol, atenolol) as these slow conduction and can precipitate complete heart block in patients with baseline bundle branch block
options.C: Calcium channel blockers (verapamil, diltiazem) as these can worsen right ventricular dysfunction and precipitate arrhythmogenic right ventricular cardiomyopathy
options.D: Digitalis glycosides (digoxin) as these increase vagal tone and can trigger bradycardia-dependent ventricular arrhythmias

mcqs.explanation: This patient has Brugada syndrome, a cardiac channelopathy characterised by abnormal sodium channel function (most commonly due to SCN5A gene mutations) that predisposes to polymorphic ventricular tachycardia and ventricular fibrillation, typically during rest or sleep. The diagnosis is supported by: (1) Characteristic type 1 Brugada ECG pattern - coved-type ST elevation ≥2 mm in ≥1 right precordial lead (V1-V2), followed by negative T wave; (2) Clinical features - syncope suggestive of arrhythmia, family history of sudden death in young relative (brother died aged 28, concerning for inherited arrhythmia syndrome); (3) Structurally normal heart on echocardiography; (4) Events occurring at rest (walking to car, not during exertion). Brugada syndrome affects approximately 1 in 2,000 people, is more common in males (8-10:1 ratio) and Southeast Asian populations, and accounts for 4-12% of sudden cardiac deaths in structurally normal hearts. The pathophysiology involves abnormal sodium channel function in the right ventricular epicardium, leading to heterogeneous repolarisation and phase 2 re-entry, which can trigger VF. Class Ic antiarrhythmic drugs (flecainide, propafenone) and other sodium channel blockers are absolutely contraindicated in Brugada syndrome. These medications further block sodium channels (Nav1.5), worsening the underlying channelopathy and accentuating the Brugada ECG pattern. They can unmask a concealed ECG phenotype or convert type 2/3 patterns to type 1, and critically, can precipitate ventricular fibrillation. In fact, intravenous flecainide or ajmaline is used as a diagnostic provocation test in patients with suspected Brugada but non-diagnostic ECG - a positive test (unmasking type 1 pattern) confirms diagnosis but must be performed in monitored setting with defibrillator available. Other medications to avoid in Brugada syndrome include: (1) Sodium channel blockers - all class I antiarrhythmics (quinidine is exception - actually therapeutic in Brugada), local anaesthetics (bupivacaine, lignocaine in high doses), tricyclic antidepressants (amitriptyline, desipramine); (2) Other drugs that can unmask or exacerbate phenotype - alcohol in excess, cocaine, cannabis, certain antihistamines, propofol (anaesthesia risk). A comprehensive list is maintained at www.brugadadrugs.org. Option B (beta-blockers) is incorrect - while the ECG shows RBBB pattern, this is part of the Brugada phenotype, not true conduction disease. Beta-blockers are not contraindicated and may actually be beneficial by reducing sympathetic triggers for arrhythmia. They do not cause heart block in Brugada syndrome unless there is concurrent AV nodal disease. Option C (calcium channel blockers) is incorrect. While this patient has an RBBB pattern, there is no evidence of arrhythmogenic right ventricular cardiomyopathy (ARVC) - echocardiography is normal, ECG shows ST elevation (not T wave inversion typical of ARVC), and clinical presentation is consistent with Brugada. Calcium channel blockers are not contraindicated in Brugada syndrome. Option D (digoxin) is incorrect. While digoxin can increase vagal tone, it is not specifically contraindicated in Brugada syndrome. The primary risk in Brugada is inappropriate sodium channel blockade, not vagal enhancement. Management of Brugada syndrome: (1) Risk stratification - this patient is high risk due to syncope (likely arrhythmic) and family history of sudden death, warranting ICD implantation for primary prevention; (2) Lifestyle advice - avoid excessive alcohol, avoid fever (antipyretics promptly if febrile as fever can trigger VF in Brugada), avoid implicated medications; (3) Family screening - first-degree relatives should have ECG screening and consider genetic testing if mutation identified; (4) Genetic counselling - 20-30% of Brugada patients have identifiable SCN5A mutation; (5) ICD programming - appropriate therapy for VF, avoid inappropriate shocks for sinus tachycardia. Differential diagnoses: (1) Arrhythmogenic right ventricular cardiomyopathy (ARVC) - usually shows T wave inversion in V1-V3, epsilon waves, structural RV changes on echo/MRI; (2) Early repolarisation syndrome - ST elevation in inferior/lateral leads, J-point elevation, different clinical presentation; (3) Pericarditis - diffuse ST elevation, PR depression, pleuritic chest pain; (4) Acute MI - would have ischaemic symptoms, troponin elevation. Risk stratification criteria: Spontaneous type 1 ECG plus one of: (1) Documented VF/polymorphic VT; (2) Syncope likely due to arrhythmia; (3) Family history of sudden death <45 years; (4) Inducible VF on electrophysiology study (controversial). This patient meets criteria 1, 2 and 3, indicating high risk requiring ICD. Teaching points: Brugada ECG pattern can be dynamic (present intermittently), may be unmasked by fever or sodium channel blockers, predominantly affects males, syncope in Brugada is arrhythmic until proven otherwise. Safety: Always check www.brugadadrugs.org before prescribing in known Brugada patients, educate patient about medication risks, provide medical alert card/bracelet, counsel about driving restrictions post-ICD.
mcqs.summary: Brugada syndrome patients must avoid Class Ic antiarrhythmics (flecainide, propafenone) and sodium channel blockers - these worsen the channelopathy and can precipitate VF. Check www.brugadadrugs.org before prescribing. High-risk patients need ICD.

question.scenario: A 19-year-old female university student presents to student health services with recurrent episodes of palpitations and dizziness. Episodes last 2-5 minutes and are triggered by sudden loud noises (alarm clocks, car horns) or emotional stress. She has had these episodes since childhood but they have increased in frequency recently during exam period. She denies syncope but reports one near-syncopal episode during a fire alarm. Family history is significant: her father has a 'heart rhythm problem' (details unknown) and her paternal aunt died suddenly aged 24 while swimming. Examination: HR 68 bpm regular, BP 118/70 mmHg, cardiovascular examination normal. ECG shows sinus rhythm with QTc of 490 milliseconds (corrected for heart rate using Bazett's formula; upper limit of normal is 460 ms in women). There are broad-based T waves in the lateral leads.
question.stem: Given the likely diagnosis of congenital long QT syndrome (LQTS), which medication class poses the greatest risk to this patient and should be strictly avoided?

options.A: QT-prolonging medications including macrolide antibiotics (erythromycin, azithromycin), fluoroquinolones (moxifloxacin), antipsychotics (haloperidol, quetiapine), antiemetics (ondansetron), and certain antidepressants (citalopram, escitalopram)
options.B: Non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs) as these can precipitate heart failure and worsen arrhythmia risk in patients with prolonged QT interval
options.C: Oral contraceptive pills containing oestrogen, as these increase QT interval duration through hormonal effects on cardiac repolarisation
options.D: Antihistamines (cetirizine, loratadine) as these cause sedation and can mask warning symptoms of impending arrhythmia

mcqs.explanation: This patient has congenital long QT syndrome (LQTS), an inherited channelopathy affecting cardiac repolarisation that predisposes to torsades de pointes (a polymorphic ventricular tachycardia) and sudden cardiac death. The diagnosis is supported by: (1) Prolonged QTc interval (490 ms; diagnostic threshold >480 ms in women, >470 ms in men using Bazett's formula, though Fridericia or Framingham formulas may be more accurate); (2) Triggered symptoms - palpitations precipitated by auditory stimuli (alarm clocks, car horns) are classic for LQTS type 2 (LQT2, KCNH2 gene mutation affecting IKr potassium channels); emotional stress can trigger LQT1 and LQT2; (3) Strong family history - father with 'heart rhythm problem' (likely also LQTS) and sudden death in young paternal aunt while swimming (exercise-triggered sudden death suggests LQT1); (4) Childhood onset; (5) Female sex (longer baseline QT, higher risk of torsades de pointes, particularly LQT2). LQTS affects approximately 1 in 2,000 people and is caused by mutations in genes encoding cardiac ion channels (most commonly KCNQ1 [LQT1], KCNH2 [LQT2], or SCN5A [LQT3]). QT-prolonging medications are absolutely contraindicated in patients with congenital LQTS as they further prolong the QT interval and dramatically increase risk of torsades de pointes and sudden cardiac death. The mechanism involves additional blockade of IKr potassium channels (particularly hERG/KCNH2 channels), compounding the underlying genetic repolarisation defect. High-risk medications include: (1) Antibiotics - macrolides (erythromycin, clarithromycin, azithromycin), fluoroquinolones (moxifloxacin, ciprofloxacin), azole antifungals (fluconazole); (2) Antipsychotics - typical (haloperidol, chlorpromazine) and atypical (quetiapine, ziprasidone, risperidone); (3) Antidepressants - selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors (citalopram, escitalopram), tricyclics (amitriptyline, imipramine); (4) Antiemetics - ondansetron, domperidone, metoclopramide; (5) Cardiovascular drugs - amiodarone, sotalol, quinidine, disopyramide; (6) Other - methadone, certain antihistamines (astemizole, terfenadine - now withdrawn), chloroquine/hydroxychloroquine. This is particularly relevant for this university student who may be prescribed antibiotics for common infections (eg, erythromycin for acne, azithromycin for respiratory infection) or ondansetron for nausea - all pose serious risk. A comprehensive list of QT-prolonging drugs is maintained at www.crediblemeds.org (CredibleMeds database), which categorises drugs by risk level (known risk, possible risk, conditional risk). All prescribers should check this database before prescribing to LQTS patients. Option B (NSAIDs) is incorrect. While NSAIDs can precipitate heart failure in patients with impaired LV function, they do not prolong QT interval and are not contraindicated in LQTS. Standard NSAIDs like ibuprofen can be used safely. Option C (oral contraceptive pills) is partially correct but not the primary concern. Oestrogen can cause mild QT prolongation (5-10 ms), and there is some evidence that hormonal fluctuations during menstrual cycle affect QT duration in women with LQT2. However, the effect is modest and OCPs are not absolutely contraindicated - the decision should be individualised based on baseline QTc, symptom control, and alternative contraceptive options. Progesterone-only contraceptives may be preferred. The far greater risk is QT-prolonging medications (Option A). Option D (antihistamines) is partially correct. First-generation antihistamines (promethazine, diphenhydramine) cause sedation but do not significantly prolong QT. However, certain older antihistamines (astemizole, terfenadine) were withdrawn from market due to QT prolongation and torsades de pointes risk - these are now unavailable. Modern second-generation antihistamines (cetirizine, loratadine, fexofenadine) do not significantly prolong QT and can be used safely in LQTS. Sedation is not a primary concern for arrhythmia risk. Management of congenital LQTS: (1) Lifestyle modifications - avoid QT-prolonging drugs (provide list and medical alert bracelet), avoid loud alarm clocks and jarring noises (especially LQT2), avoid competitive sports (especially swimming for LQT1), ensure adequate potassium intake (maintain K+ >4.0 mmol/L); (2) Beta-blocker therapy - nadolol or propranolol (not metoprolol which is less effective) is first-line for all symptomatic LQTS patients and asymptomatic patients with QTc >500 ms; beta-blockers reduce risk of cardiac events by 60-70%, particularly in LQT1 and LQT2; (3) ICD implantation - indicated for: (a) cardiac arrest survivor; (b) syncope despite beta-blocker therapy; (c) LQT3 (less responsive to beta-blockers); (d) QTc >500 ms with strong family history; (4) Genetic testing - confirm subtype (LQT1, LQT2, LQT3, etc.) to guide therapy and enable family cascade screening; (5) Family screening - first-degree relatives should have ECG, consider genetic testing if proband mutation identified; (6) Electrolyte monitoring - correct hypokalaemia/hypomagnesaemia aggressively (potassium >4.0 mmol/L, magnesium >0.8 mmol/L); (7) Avoid triggers - LQT1 triggered by exercise/swimming, LQT2 by auditory stimuli/emotion, LQT3 by bradycardia/sleep. Specific considerations for this patient: (1) Likely LQT2 (auditory triggers) but swimming death in aunt suggests possible LQT1 - genetic testing warranted; (2) University student - counsel about alcohol (can prolong QT), recreational drugs (cocaine, amphetamines prolong QT), stress management during exams; (3) Young woman - counsel about pregnancy (LQTS increases risk of postpartum cardiac events, particularly LQT2), continue beta-blockers during pregnancy (safe), avoid epidural analgesia with epinephrine (can prolong QT); (4) Medication safety - provide written list of drugs to avoid, medical alert bracelet, educate about checking CredibleMeds database. Teaching points: QTc calculation using Bazett's formula (QTc = QT / √RR interval), but Bazett's overestimates QTc at high heart rates - use Fridericia formula (QTc = QT / ∛RR) for more accuracy; normal QTc <450 ms (men), <460 ms (women); borderline 450-470 ms (men), 460-480 ms (women); prolonged >470 ms (men), >480 ms (women). Schwartz score for LQTS diagnosis combines QTc, clinical history, family history. Differential diagnoses: (1) Acquired long QT (drug-induced, electrolyte disturbances) - excluded by childhood onset and family history; (2) Other channelopathies - Brugada syndrome (different ECG pattern), catecholaminergic polymorphic VT (normal QT, exercise-induced); (3) Hypertrophic cardiomyopathy - would show LVH on ECG/echo. Safety: This patient requires immediate beta-blocker initiation (nadolol 20-40 mg daily, titrate to effect), genetic testing, family screening, medication education, driving restrictions if syncopal (6 months restriction in Australia), avoid competitive swimming until risk-stratified. Cardiology/electrophysiology referral for ongoing management and ICD consideration if high-risk features.
mcqs.summary: Congenital long QT syndrome patients must avoid ALL QT-prolonging medications (macrolides, fluoroquinolones, antipsychotics, ondansetron, certain antidepressants). Check www.crediblemeds.org before prescribing. First-line treatment: beta-blockers (nadolol/propranolol). Provide drug avoidance list and medical alert bracelet.

question.scenario: A 28-year-old woman presents to the Emergency Department at Young District Hospital with a 30-minute history of sudden-onset palpitations. She describes the sensation as her 'heart racing' that started while sitting at her desk at work. No chest pain, dyspnoea, or syncope. Past medical history unremarkable, no regular medications. Vital signs: HR 185 bpm (regular), BP 115/75 mmHg, RR 18/min, SpO2 98% on room air, temperature 36.8°C. Patient appears anxious but alert and oriented. ECG shows narrow complex regular tachycardia at 185 bpm with no clearly visible P waves. Cardiovascular examination: JVP not elevated, heart sounds rapid but dual with no murmurs, chest clear, no peripheral oedema.
question.stem: What is the most appropriate initial management strategy?

options.A: Instruct patient to perform Valsalva manoeuvre, followed by carotid sinus massage if unsuccessful
options.B: Administer adenosine 6 mg rapid IV push followed by 20 mL saline flush
options.C: Administer metoprolol 5 mg IV over 2 minutes
options.D: Perform immediate synchronised DC cardioversion at 100 joules
options.E: Administer amiodarone 300 mg IV over 20 minutes

mcqs.explanation:
CLINICAL REASONING:

This patient presents with classic features of paroxysmal supraventricular tachycardia (SVT). The ECG findings of narrow complex regular tachycardia (QRS <120 ms) at 185 bpm with no visible P waves suggests either atrioventricular nodal re-entrant tachycardia (AVNRT, most common at 60%) or atrioventricular re-entrant tachycardia (AVRT via accessory pathway, 30% of SVT cases). The sudden onset while at rest, young age, structurally normal heart, and haemodynamic stability are typical presentations.

AUSTRALIAN GUIDELINE APPROACH (eTG Cardiovascular 2025):

For haemodynamically stable SVT (systolic BP >90 mmHg, conscious, no chest pain), the stepwise management is:
1. VAGAL MANOEUVRES FIRST (Option A - CORRECT): These increase parasympathetic tone, temporarily blocking AV node conduction and terminating re-entrant circuits. Valsalva manoeuvre (strain against closed glottis for 15 seconds) has 20-40% success rate. If unsuccessful, carotid sinus massage (5-10 seconds, one side at a time, after auscultating for bruits) adds 10-20% success. These are safe, non-invasive, and recommended as first-line by Australian Resuscitation Council guidelines.

2. ADENOSINE if vagal manoeuvres fail (Option B): Adenosine 6 mg rapid IV push (followed by 20 mL saline flush, arm elevated) is second-line for stable SVT. Success rate 90-95%. Can repeat with 12 mg if 6 mg ineffective. However, this is NOT first-line - vagal manoeuvres should be attempted first as they avoid medication side effects (chest tightness, bronchospasm, flushing).

3. IV beta-blockers/calcium channel blockers (Option C): Metoprolol 5 mg IV is third-line for rate control if adenosine contraindicated or fails. Slower onset than adenosine, less effective for acute termination. Reserved for patients where vagal manoeuvres and adenosine unsuccessful.

4. DC cardioversion (Option D): Only for haemodynamically unstable SVT (shock, syncope, myocardial ischaemia, acute heart failure). This patient has BP 115/75 mmHg and is alert - NOT unstable. Cardioversion would be inappropriate and exposes patient to unnecessary sedation risks.

5. Amiodarone (Option E): Not first-line for SVT. Reserved for atrial fibrillation with rapid ventricular response or when other measures fail. Has slower onset (20-30 minutes) and more side effects than adenosine.

DIFFERENTIAL DIAGNOSIS:

- AVNRT (most likely): Sudden onset, regular narrow complex, no visible P waves (buried in QRS). Accounts for 60% of paroxysmal SVT cases.
- AVRT: Similar presentation but may have retrograde P waves (RP interval short). Occurs in 30% of SVT, often in younger patients with accessory pathways.
- Atrial flutter: Would show sawtooth pattern (flutter waves) in inferior leads (II, III, aVF). Typically 2:1 conduction giving HR ~150 bpm. Not described in this ECG.
- Atrial fibrillation: Irregularly irregular rhythm with no P waves. This patient's rhythm is REGULAR, excluding AF.
- Sinus tachycardia: Would have visible upright P waves in lead II, gradual onset/offset. Not sudden onset like this case.

AUSTRALIAN CONTEXT:

In rural NSW hospitals like Young District Hospital, immediate access to cardiology consultation may be limited. The stepwise approach (vagal → adenosine → specialist contact) is crucial. If SVT recurs or doesn't respond to initial management, telehealth consultation with tertiary centre (Wagga Base Hospital cardiology) should be initiated. Patient education about vagal manoeuvres (Valsalva, diving reflex with ice water) empowers self-management for future episodes.

SAFETY NETTING:

- If vagal manoeuvres fail after 2-3 attempts: proceed to adenosine 6 mg IV
- If patient becomes haemodynamically unstable (BP <90 mmHg, altered consciousness, chest pain): immediate DC cardioversion
- If adenosine fails or SVT recurs: consider alternative diagnoses (atrial flutter, atrial tachycardia), obtain specialist advice
- Document rhythm strips before, during, and after interventions for diagnostic clarity
- Arrange cardiology follow-up for risk stratification and consideration of catheter ablation (curative in >95% of AVNRT/AVRT cases)

MEDICOLEGAL CONSIDERATIONS:

Attempting DC cardioversion on a haemodynamically stable patient without first trying vagal manoeuvres would be considered substandard care. Australian guidelines (ARC, eTG) clearly specify the stepwise approach. Documentation should include: 'Patient haemodynamically stable, vagal manoeuvres attempted as per ARC guidelines before pharmacological intervention.'

REFERENCES:
- eTG Cardiovascular (Therapeutic Guidelines Limited, 2025): Supraventricular tachycardia management
- Australian Resuscitation Council Guideline 11.6: Advanced Life Support - Tachycardia Algorithm (2024)
- NSW Health Emergency Care Institute: Tachycardia Clinical Pathway (2024)
mcqs.summary: Haemodynamically stable SVT (narrow complex regular tachycardia, no visible P waves, likely AVNRT) requires stepwise management: vagal manoeuvres FIRST (Valsalva, carotid massage - safe, non-invasive, 20-40% success), then adenosine 6 mg IV if unsuccessful (90-95% success), then IV beta-blockers/calcium channel blockers if needed. DC cardioversion reserved for unstable patients only. Australian guidelines (eTG, ARC) mandate vagal manoeuvres as first-line before medications.

question.scenario: The same 28-year-old woman from the previous case has now performed two Valsalva manoeuvres (each 15 seconds) without effect. Carotid sinus massage was attempted on the right side for 10 seconds (after auscultating for bruits - none present) but the tachycardia persists. Repeat vital signs: HR 182 bpm (regular), BP 110/70 mmHg, RR 20/min, SpO2 98% on room air. Patient remains alert and oriented but reports feeling 'exhausted' from the ongoing palpitations. No chest pain or dyspnoea. Repeat ECG unchanged: narrow complex regular tachycardia at 182 bpm. IV access established (18G cannula in left antecubital fossa). You have adenosine ampoules (6 mg/2 mL) available, along with cardiac monitoring and resuscitation equipment.
question.stem: What is the most appropriate next step in management?

options.A: Attempt left-sided carotid sinus massage as the right side was unsuccessful
options.B: Administer adenosine 6 mg rapid IV push followed immediately by 20 mL normal saline flush, with continuous ECG monitoring
options.C: Administer verapamil 5 mg IV over 2 minutes
options.D: Administer metoprolol 5 mg IV over 2 minutes
options.E: Proceed to synchronised DC cardioversion at 100 joules under procedural sedation

mcqs.explanation:
CLINICAL REASONING:

Vagal manoeuvres have failed (Valsalva x2, carotid massage right side), and the patient remains haemodynamically stable (BP 110/70 mmHg, alert, no ischaemic symptoms). According to Australian Resuscitation Council (ARC) guidelines and eTG Cardiovascular, the next step in the stepwise management of stable SVT is ADENOSINE.

ADENOSINE ADMINISTRATION (Option B - CORRECT):

Adenosine is a purine nucleoside that causes transient complete AV block (duration 10-15 seconds), terminating re-entrant tachycardias (AVNRT, AVRT) that depend on AV nodal conduction. Key technical points for safe administration:

1. DOSE: 6 mg rapid IV push (into large proximal vein - antecubital fossa ideal). If unsuccessful after 1-2 minutes, can repeat with 12 mg, then 18 mg (maximum). First dose success rate 60-70%, second dose (12 mg) increases cumulative success to 90-95%.

2. TECHNIQUE: CRITICAL - must give rapid IV push (over 1-2 seconds) followed IMMEDIATELY by 20 mL normal saline flush (also rapid push), with arm elevated. Adenosine has half-life <10 seconds, so slow administration or delay in flushing results in drug degradation before reaching heart.

3. MONITORING: Continuous ECG monitoring essential. Adenosine causes transient complete heart block (asystole 3-15 seconds) which can be alarming but is expected and self-limiting. Warn patient: 'You will feel your heart stop briefly, may feel flushed or short of breath - this is normal and lasts only seconds.'

4. EXPECTED RESPONSE:
- If SVT (AVNRT/AVRT): Rhythm terminates abruptly, converts to sinus rhythm
- If atrial flutter/fibrillation: Transient AV block reveals underlying atrial rhythm (flutter waves or fibrillatory waves) - diagnostic but doesn't terminate rhythm
- If sinus tachycardia or atrial tachycardia: Brief slowing then returns to tachycardia

5. CONTRAINDICATIONS (none in this case):
- Asthma/COPD (can cause bronchospasm - use with extreme caution, have bronchodilators ready)
- Second/third-degree AV block
- Sick sinus syndrome
- Atrial fibrillation with pre-excitation (WPW with AF) - can precipitate VF
- Recent dipyridamole (potentiates adenosine)
- Theophylline (antagonises adenosine - may need higher doses)

6. SIDE EFFECTS (warn patient): Chest tightness (75%), flushing (25%), dyspnoea (15%), headache (10%). All are transient (<60 seconds) and self-limiting.

WHY OTHER OPTIONS ARE INCORRECT:

Option A (Left carotid massage): Once vagal manoeuvres have been attempted (right carotid massage done), repeating on the opposite side adds minimal benefit (<5% additional success). Prolonging vagal attempts delays definitive treatment. Australian guidelines recommend proceeding to adenosine after initial vagal manoeuvres fail, not exhaustively trying all vagal techniques.

Option C (Verapamil IV): Calcium channel blocker effective for SVT but SECOND-LINE to adenosine. Verapamil has slower onset (5-10 minutes), longer duration of action (2-4 hours), and more haemodynamic effects (hypotension, negative inotropy) compared to adenosine (onset <30 seconds, duration <60 seconds). Australian guidelines prefer adenosine for acute termination due to its safety profile and rapid reversibility. Verapamil also CONTRAINDICATED if WPW suspected (can accelerate accessory pathway conduction).

Option D (Metoprolol IV): Beta-blocker less effective than adenosine for acute SVT termination. Provides rate control rather than rhythm termination. Reserved for cases where adenosine contraindicated (asthma) or fails. Slower onset than adenosine, longer duration, more side effects (hypotension, bradycardia, bronchospasm in asthmatics).

Option E (DC cardioversion): Patient remains haemodynamically STABLE (BP 110/70 mmHg, alert, no chest pain). Cardioversion is invasive, requires procedural sedation (propofol/midazolam), and carries risks (aspiration, hypotension, post-cardioversion arrhythmias). Australian guidelines reserve cardioversion for unstable SVT (shock, syncope, severe heart failure, myocardial ischaemia). This patient's only symptom is 'exhaustion' - not an indication for cardioversion when safer medical options (adenosine) remain untried.

AUSTRALIAN CONTEXT (RURAL PRACTICE):

At Young District Hospital, adenosine should be stocked in Emergency Department resuscitation bay. If adenosine unavailable (rare but possible in rural settings), options include:
- Verapamil 5 mg IV as alternative (if no WPW suspected)
- Retrieval to tertiary centre (Wagga Base Hospital) for cardioversion if medications fail
- Telehealth consultation with cardiology for guidance

DOCUMENTATION:

Document: 'Vagal manoeuvres unsuccessful (Valsalva x2, right carotid massage x1). Patient remains haemodynamically stable. Adenosine 6 mg IV administered as per ARC guidelines at [time]. Patient warned of transient chest tightness/flushing. Continuous ECG monitoring. [Outcome: successful termination / required second dose 12 mg / unsuccessful - specialist consulted].'

SAFETY NETTING:

- If adenosine 6 mg unsuccessful: repeat with 12 mg after 1-2 minutes
- If 12 mg unsuccessful: consider 18 mg (maximum dose) or specialist consultation
- If rhythm terminates but recurs: consider maintenance beta-blocker or calcium channel blocker, arrange urgent cardiology review
- If patient becomes unstable during adenosine: have resuscitation equipment ready (rare)
- If adenosine reveals atrial flutter/fibrillation: change management strategy (rate control, anticoagulation assessment)

MEDICOLEGAL:

Skipping adenosine and proceeding directly to cardioversion in a stable patient would be considered substandard care. Australian guidelines (ARC Guideline 11.6, eTG) mandate stepwise approach: vagal → adenosine → specialist/cardioversion. Document why each step was appropriate.

REFERENCES:
- Australian Resuscitation Council Guideline 11.6: Advanced Life Support - Tachycardia (2024)
- eTG Cardiovascular: Supraventricular tachycardia (Therapeutic Guidelines Limited, 2025)
- LITFL: Adenosine administration technique (https://litfl.com/adenosine/)
mcqs.summary: After failed vagal manoeuvres, stable SVT requires adenosine 6 mg rapid IV push followed immediately by 20 mL saline flush (arm elevated). Adenosine causes transient AV block (10-15 seconds), terminating AVNRT/AVRT with 90-95% success (cumulative after 6 mg, 12 mg, 18 mg doses). Warn patient of transient chest tightness/flushing (<60 seconds). Continuous ECG monitoring essential. Contraindications: asthma/COPD (relative), WPW with AF, AV block. Adenosine preferred over verapamil/metoprolol due to rapid onset, short duration, safety profile. DC cardioversion reserved for unstable patients.

question.scenario: A 22-year-old male university student presents to Young District Hospital Emergency Department with a history of recurrent episodes of palpitations since age 16. Current episode started 2 hours ago during a basketball game. He describes sudden onset of rapid regular palpitations, associated with mild chest tightness and light-headedness. No syncope. Previous episodes terminated spontaneously after 10-30 minutes. Never sought medical attention before. No family history of sudden cardiac death. Non-smoker, no regular medications, no illicit drug use. Examination: HR 195 bpm (regular), BP 125/80 mmHg, RR 22/min, SpO2 99% on room air. Patient appears anxious but alert. Cardiovascular examination: JVP normal, dual heart sounds (rapid), no murmurs, chest clear, no oedema. ECG (during tachycardia): Narrow complex regular tachycardia at 195 bpm. You successfully terminate the tachycardia with adenosine. Post-conversion ECG in sinus rhythm shows: Rate 75 bpm, PR interval 100 ms (normal 120-200 ms), QRS duration 130 ms with slurred upstroke (delta wave) visible in leads I, II, V4-V6. QTc normal. No ST/T wave changes.
question.stem: What is the most likely underlying diagnosis?

options.A: Atrioventricular nodal re-entrant tachycardia (AVNRT)
options.B: Wolff-Parkinson-White syndrome
options.C: Long QT syndrome
options.D: Brugada syndrome
options.E: Atrial flutter with variable AV conduction

mcqs.explanation:
CLINICAL REASONING:

This case presents a young patient with recurrent paroxysmal SVT and characteristic ECG findings on the post-conversion rhythm strip. The key diagnostic features are:

ECG DIAGNOSTIC CRITERIA (Wolff-Parkinson-White Pattern):

1. SHORT PR INTERVAL: 100 ms (<120 ms, normal 120-200 ms)
- Indicates ventricular pre-excitation via accessory pathway (Bundle of Kent)
- Impulse bypasses AV node delay, reaching ventricles early

2. DELTA WAVE: Slurred upstroke of QRS complex
- Represents slow initial ventricular depolarisation via accessory pathway (muscle-to-muscle conduction slower than His-Purkinje system)
- Classic finding in leads I, II, V4-V6 (left-sided accessory pathways most common)

3. WIDENED QRS: 130 ms (normal <120 ms)
- Due to fusion of pre-excited ventricular activation (via accessory pathway) and normal activation (via AV node/His-Purkinje)
- Width depends on degree of pre-excitation

WOLFF-PARKINSON-WHITE SYNDROME (Option B - CORRECT):

Definition: WPW syndrome = WPW pattern (delta wave, short PR, wide QRS) + symptomatic tachyarrhythmias. This patient has BOTH ECG pattern AND recurrent SVT episodes, fulfilling diagnostic criteria.

PATHOPHYSIOLOGY:

WPW is caused by accessory pathway (Bundle of Kent) connecting atria directly to ventricles, bypassing AV node. Prevalence 0.1-0.3% (1-3 per 1,000). Male predominance 60%. Most commonly left-sided (left atrium to left ventricle). Creates substrate for re-entrant tachycardias:

1. ORTHODROMIC AVRT (95% of WPW tachycardias - likely this case):
- Antegrade conduction DOWN AV node → ventricles → retrograde UP accessory pathway → atria → cycle
- ECG during tachycardia: NARROW complex (ventricular activation via normal His-Purkinje)
- ECG in sinus rhythm: Shows pre-excitation (delta wave, short PR)

2. ANTIDROMIC AVRT (5% of WPW tachycardias):
- Antegrade conduction DOWN accessory pathway → ventricles (wide QRS)
- Retrograde UP AV node
- ECG during tachycardia: WIDE complex (can mimic VT)

3. ATRIAL FIBRILLATION (10-30% of WPW patients develop AF):
- DANGEROUS: Accessory pathway lacks AV node's protective decremental conduction
- Can conduct rapid atrial rates (>300 bpm) directly to ventricles → degenerates to VF
- Leading cause of sudden cardiac death in WPW (rare, 0.1% risk)

CLINICAL FEATURES (all present in this case):

- Young age at presentation (teens-20s typically, 70% diagnosed by age 40)
- Recurrent palpitations since adolescence (age 16 in this case)
- Exercise-triggered (basketball game - increased sympathetic tone)
- Sudden onset/termination (classic for re-entrant SVT)
- Responsive to adenosine (terminates AVRT by blocking AV node)
- Delta wave visible on baseline ECG post-conversion

WHY OTHER OPTIONS ARE INCORRECT:

Option A (AVNRT): Atrioventricular nodal re-entrant tachycardia accounts for 60% of paroxysmal SVT but does NOT cause delta waves or short PR interval on baseline ECG. AVNRT involves re-entry within AV node (fast and slow pathways), not an accessory pathway. Baseline ECG in AVNRT patients is entirely normal between episodes. This patient's ECG shows clear pre-excitation (delta wave, PR 100 ms) - diagnostic for WPW, not AVNRT.

Option C (Long QT syndrome): LQTS causes polymorphic VT (torsades de pointes), NOT narrow complex SVT. ECG shows prolonged QTc (>460 ms women, >440 ms men) and abnormal T wave morphology. This patient's QTc is NORMAL, excluding LQTS. Also, LQTS presents with syncope or cardiac arrest, not palpitations.

Option D (Brugada syndrome): Brugada causes polymorphic VT/VF, typically during sleep (not exercise). ECG shows coved ST elevation in V1-V3 (Type 1 pattern), NOT delta waves or short PR. This patient's ECG has no ST elevation. Brugada does not cause narrow complex SVT.

Option E (Atrial flutter with variable conduction): Flutter produces sawtooth flutter waves (best seen in inferior leads II, III, aVF) and typically regular 2:1 conduction (atrial rate 300 bpm → ventricular rate 150 bpm). Does NOT cause delta waves or short PR on baseline ECG. This patient's post-conversion ECG shows sinus rhythm with pre-excitation, not flutter.

AUSTRALIAN MANAGEMENT:

1. EMERGENCY (completed): SVT terminated with adenosine (appropriate)

2. RISK STRATIFICATION (urgent):
- Refer to cardiology (within 2 weeks for symptomatic WPW)
- Exercise ECG or electrophysiology study to assess accessory pathway refractoriness
- High-risk features: Short refractory period (<250 ms), multiple pathways, previous AF

3. DEFINITIVE TREATMENT:
- Catheter ablation (radiofrequency or cryoablation) - CURATIVE in >95% of cases
- First-line for symptomatic WPW (Class I recommendation, ACC/AHA/ESC guidelines)
- Complication rate <1% (heart block, tamponade, stroke)
- Alternative: Antiarrhythmic drugs (flecainide, propafenone) - less effective, lifelong

4. LIFESTYLE ADVICE:
- Avoid competitive sports until risk stratified (Australian Heart Foundation recommendation)
- Educate on vagal manoeuvres for self-termination of SVT
- Avoid AV nodal blockers if AF develops (verapamil, diltiazem, beta-blockers, digoxin, adenosine OK for SVT but NOT for AF in WPW)

5. SAFETY NETTING:
- If develops irregular broad complex tachycardia (suggests AF with pre-excitation) → URGENT cardioversion, DO NOT give AV nodal blockers (can accelerate pathway, cause VF)
- Return to ED if palpitations >30 minutes, syncope, chest pain

RURAL CONTEXT (Young District Hospital):

- Cardiology referral via telehealth to Wagga Base Hospital or Sydney tertiary centre
- If develops AF with pre-excitation: retrieval to tertiary centre (requires specialist management)
- Patient education critical as definitive ablation may require travel to metropolitan centre

MEDICOLEGAL:

Failing to recognise WPW pattern on post-conversion ECG and refer for cardiology assessment would be negligent. WPW carries risk of sudden death (0.1% annually, highest in young active males). Documentation should state: 'Post-conversion ECG shows WPW pattern (delta wave, short PR). Patient advised of diagnosis, risks discussed, urgent cardiology referral arranged.'

DIFFERENTIAL DIAGNOSIS OF DELTA WAVE:

- WPW syndrome (most common)
- Ventricular pacing (pacing spike visible)
- Bundle branch block (no short PR interval)
- Ventricular pre-excitation due to other causes (rare: Mahaim fibres, fasciculoventricular pathways)

REFERENCES:
- eTG Cardiovascular: Wolff-Parkinson-White syndrome (Therapeutic Guidelines Limited, 2025)
- European Heart Rhythm Association: 2019 Guidelines on supraventricular tachycardia
- Australian Heart Foundation: Pre-participation screening for sudden cardiac death (2023)
- Cardiac Society of Australia and New Zealand: Arrhythmia management guidelines
mcqs.summary: Wolff-Parkinson-White syndrome diagnosed by: (1) Short PR interval (<120 ms), (2) Delta wave (slurred QRS upstroke), (3) Widened QRS (>120 ms), (4) Recurrent SVT (orthodromic AVRT - narrow complex during tachycardia, pre-excitation on baseline ECG). WPW caused by accessory pathway (Bundle of Kent) bypassing AV node. Risk: 10-30% develop AF → rapid ventricular rates via accessory pathway → VF (0.1% sudden death annually). Management: Acute SVT responds to adenosine/vagal manoeuvres. Definitive treatment: Catheter ablation (>95% cure rate, first-line for symptomatic cases). AVOID AV nodal blockers if AF develops (verapamil, diltiazem, beta-blockers, digoxin). Urgent cardiology referral for risk stratification.

question.scenario: A 35-year-old man with known Wolff-Parkinson-White syndrome (diagnosed 5 years ago, declined ablation) presents to Young District Hospital Emergency Department with palpitations and pre-syncope. Episode started 45 minutes ago after drinking 3 cups of coffee. He reports his heart feels 'chaotic' rather than the usual rapid regular palpitations he experiences with SVT episodes. No chest pain but feels light-headed. Past episodes of orthodromic AVRT have responded to vagal manoeuvres or adenosine. No other medical history, no regular medications. Examination: Patient appears anxious and diaphoretic. HR 220 bpm (IRREGULAR), BP 95/60 mmHg, RR 24/min, SpO2 97% on room air. Cardiovascular: JVP elevated, heart sounds rapid and irregular, chest clear to auscultation, no peripheral oedema. ECG shows: Irregularly irregular broad complex tachycardia (QRS 180-200 ms) at rate varying 200-240 bpm. QRS morphology varies beat-to-beat. No organised P waves visible.
question.stem: What is the most appropriate immediate management? (Select the option that could SAVE the patient's life)

options.A: Administer adenosine 6 mg rapid IV push to terminate the tachycardia
options.B: Administer metoprolol 5 mg IV to slow ventricular rate
options.C: Administer procainamide 10 mg/kg IV over 20 minutes OR immediate synchronised DC cardioversion
options.D: Administer digoxin 500 microgram IV loading dose
options.E: Administer diltiazem 0.25 mg/kg IV over 2 minutes

mcqs.explanation:
CLINICAL REASONING - LIFE-THREATENING SCENARIO:

This patient presents with the most dangerous arrhythmia complication of Wolff-Parkinson-White syndrome: ATRIAL FIBRILLATION WITH PRE-EXCITATION (AF-WPW). This is a medical emergency with high risk of deterioration to ventricular fibrillation and sudden cardiac death within minutes.

ECG DIAGNOSTIC FEATURES (AF with Pre-Excitation via Accessory Pathway):

1. IRREGULARLY IRREGULAR rhythm (characteristic of AF)
2. BROAD complex (wide QRS 180-200 ms) - ventricular pre-excitation via accessory pathway
3. VERY rapid ventricular rate (200-240 bpm) - accessory pathway conducting AF without AV nodal protective delay
4. VARIABLE QRS morphology beat-to-beat - varying degree of fusion between pre-excited conduction (via pathway) and normal conduction (via AV node)
5. No organised P waves (fibrillatory waves may be visible)

PATHOPHYSIOLOGY - WHY THIS IS DEADLY:

Normal Scenario: AF with normal heart → AV node limits ventricular rate to 100-180 bpm due to decremental conduction (protective mechanism)

WPW Scenario: AF with accessory pathway → Pathway has NO decremental conduction → Conducts atrial rates >300 bpm directly to ventricles → Extremely rapid ventricular rates (200-350 bpm) → Short diastolic filling time → Reduced cardiac output → Hypotension → Myocardial ischaemia → Deterioration to ventricular fibrillation (VF) → SUDDEN CARDIAC DEATH

This is the mechanism of sudden death in WPW (accounts for 80% of WPW-related deaths). Risk factors: Short pathway refractory period (<250 ms), young males, triggered by caffeine/alcohol/sympathomimetics.

CRITICAL MANAGEMENT PRINCIPLE:

**DO NOT USE AV NODAL BLOCKING AGENTS** (adenosine, beta-blockers, calcium channel blockers, digoxin)

Why? AV nodal blockers BLOCK the AV node but ENHANCE accessory pathway conduction by:
1. Increasing refractoriness of AV node → More impulses diverted to accessory pathway
2. Shortening accessory pathway refractory period (paradoxical effect)
3. Result: FASTER ventricular rates via accessory pathway → VF → Death

CORRECT MANAGEMENT (Option C):

TWO first-line options (both acceptable, choice depends on clinical stability and drug availability):

1. PROCAINAMIDE IV (if haemodynamically stable or borderline):
- Dose: 10-15 mg/kg IV over 20-60 minutes (max rate 50 mg/min)
- For 70 kg patient: 700 mg-1050 mg IV
- Mechanism: Blocks sodium channels, PROLONGS accessory pathway refractory period, slows conduction through pathway
- Success rate: 80-90% for terminating AF-WPW or slowing rate
- Monitoring: BP (can cause hypotension - slow infusion if BP drops), ECG (watch for QRS widening >50% baseline → stop infusion)
- Alternative: Amiodarone 300 mg IV over 20 minutes (also blocks accessory pathway but slower onset than procainamide)

2. SYNCHRONISED DC CARDIOVERSION (if haemodynamically unstable):
- Indications: SBP <90 mmHg, altered consciousness, chest pain (myocardial ischaemia), acute heart failure, rate >250 bpm with severe symptoms
- Energy: Start 200 joules biphasic (or 360 joules monophasic)
- Synchronised mode essential (prevents shocking on T wave → VF)
- Sedation: Procedural sedation with propofol or midazolam + fentanyl (if time permits)
- Success rate: >95% for immediate termination

THIS CASE: Patient has BP 95/60 mmHg (borderline hypotensive), pre-syncope, HR 220 bpm → Either procainamide OR cardioversion acceptable. Many emergency physicians would proceed directly to cardioversion given borderline haemodynamics (BP <100 mmHg systolic is often threshold for immediate cardioversion). However, if patient mentating well and procainamide available, trial of procainamide with cardioversion readiness is reasonable.

WHY OTHER OPTIONS ARE DANGEROUS/WRONG:

Option A (Adenosine): **CONTRAINDICATED** in AF-WPW. Adenosine blocks AV node → diverts ALL conduction to accessory pathway → can INCREASE ventricular rate to >300 bpm → precipitates VF → DEATH. Multiple case reports of adenosine-induced VF in WPW. This is tested knowledge on FRACP, AMC exams - must know not to use adenosine in broad complex irregular tachycardia suggestive of pre-excited AF.

Option B (Metoprolol): **CONTRAINDICATED** in AF-WPW. Beta-blocker blocks AV node, enhances accessory pathway conduction → faster ventricular rates → VF. Additionally, metoprolol causes hypotension (patient already BP 95/60 mmHg) and negative inotropy → cardiogenic shock.

Option D (Digoxin): **CONTRAINDICATED** in AF-WPW. Digoxin shortens accessory pathway refractory period and blocks AV node → INCREASES conduction via accessory pathway → VF. Digoxin-induced VF in WPW well-documented. Digoxin also has slow onset (hours) - inappropriate for acute emergency.

Option E (Diltiazem): **CONTRAINDICATED** in AF-WPW. Calcium channel blocker blocks AV node, enhances accessory pathway conduction → VF. Same mechanism as metoprolol/adenosine.

AUSTRALIAN CONTEXT:

At Young District Hospital (rural NSW), procainamide may not be readily available (less commonly stocked than amiodarone). If procainamide unavailable:
- Use amiodarone 300 mg IV over 20 minutes (second choice, slower onset)
- Proceed to DC cardioversion (safest, most effective)
- Consult retrieval service (NSW Ambulance Aeromedical) for transfer to tertiary centre if patient deteriorates or recurs after cardioversion

SAFETY NETTING:

- If procainamide fails: Immediate DC cardioversion
- If patient deteriorates (SBP <80 mmHg, altered consciousness): Skip procainamide, immediate cardioversion
- After rhythm control: Urgent cardiology referral for catheter ablation (AF will recur if pathway not ablated)
- If VF develops: Immediate unsynchronised defibrillation 200 joules, CPR, ACLS protocol

POST-CARDIOVERSION MANAGEMENT:

1. Admit to monitored bed (telemetry or HDU/ICU)
2. Anticoagulation assessment (if AF >48 hours - unlikely in this acute presentation)
3. URGENT cardiology referral for catheter ablation (Class I recommendation - patient has now developed life-threatening arrhythmia, ablation mandatory)
4. Avoid triggers: Cease caffeine, alcohol, sympathomimetics
5. Do NOT discharge on AV nodal blockers (beta-blockers, calcium channel blockers, digoxin) - contraindicated in WPW until pathway ablated

MEDICOLEGAL:

Administering adenosine, beta-blockers, calcium channel blockers, or digoxin to a patient with broad complex irregular tachycardia (suggestive of AF-WPW) would be considered gross negligence. This is core emergency medicine knowledge. If patient deteriorates to VF after inappropriate AV nodal blocker administration, this would be indefensible in court. Documentation must show: 'Broad complex irregular tachycardia in known WPW patient - likely pre-excited AF. AV nodal blockers AVOIDED (risk of VF). Procainamide 700 mg IV commenced / DC cardioversion performed.'

DIFFERENTIAL DIAGNOSIS OF BROAD COMPLEX IRREGULAR TACHYCARDIA:

1. Pre-excited AF (WPW + AF) - this case, most likely given known WPW
2. Polymorphic VT (torsades de pointes) - QRS axis/morphology changes continuously, usually in setting of long QT
3. AF with bundle branch block - QRS wide but consistent morphology (not varying), rate typically <180 bpm
4. AF with ventricular pacing - pacing spikes visible

RULE: Any broad complex irregular tachycardia in young patient with palpitations → Assume pre-excited AF until proven otherwise → AVOID AV nodal blockers → Use procainamide or cardioversion

REFERENCES:
- eTG Cardiovascular: Wolff-Parkinson-White syndrome - AF management (Therapeutic Guidelines Limited, 2025)
- Australian Resuscitation Council Guideline 11.6: Tachycardia algorithm - pre-excited AF (2024)
- European Heart Rhythm Association: 2019 Guidelines on SVT - WPW with AF (Class III recommendation for AV nodal blockers - meaning CONTRAINDICATED)
- Cardiac Society of Australia and New Zealand: Arrhythmia management - pre-excited AF
mcqs.summary: Atrial fibrillation with pre-excitation (AF-WPW): Irregularly irregular broad complex tachycardia (200-240 bpm) in WPW patient. LIFE-THREATENING - can deteriorate to VF. Accessory pathway conducts rapid AF rates without AV nodal protection. **CRITICAL: DO NOT USE AV NODAL BLOCKERS** (adenosine, beta-blockers, calcium channel blockers, digoxin) - they block AV node, enhance accessory pathway conduction, INCREASE VF risk. CORRECT management: (1) Procainamide 10-15 mg/kg IV (blocks pathway, slows/terminates AF) OR (2) Immediate DC cardioversion if unstable (SBP <90 mmHg). Amiodarone alternative if procainamide unavailable. Post-cardioversion: Urgent ablation referral (prevents recurrence).

question.scenario: A 68-year-old woman presents to Young District Hospital Emergency Department with a 3-day history of palpitations and dyspnoea on exertion. She describes her heartbeat as 'rapid and regular but fluttering.' No chest pain or syncope. Past medical history: Hypertension (well-controlled on perindopril 5 mg daily), osteoarthritis. No previous arrhythmias. Non-smoker, alcohol 1 standard drink weekly. Examination: HR 150 bpm (regular), BP 135/85 mmHg, RR 18/min, SpO2 96% on room air, afebrile. Cardiovascular: JVP normal, dual heart sounds (rapid, regular), systolic murmur 2/6 at apex (known mitral regurgitation - mild on echo 2 years ago), chest clear, mild bilateral ankle oedema (chronic). ECG shows: Regular narrow complex tachycardia at 150 bpm. In leads II, III, aVF, there is a characteristic 'sawtooth' pattern with regular negative deflections at rate ~300/min. No clearly defined P waves. QRS complexes occur every second flutter wave (2:1 conduction ratio). No delta waves, normal QRS duration (90 ms).
question.stem: What is the most likely diagnosis?

options.A: Atrial fibrillation with rapid ventricular response
options.B: Atrial flutter with 2:1 atrioventricular conduction
options.C: Sinus tachycardia
options.D: Atrioventricular nodal re-entrant tachycardia (AVNRT)

mcqs.explanation:
CLINICAL REASONING:

This patient presents with classic clinical and ECG features of atrial flutter with 2:1 atrioventricular conduction. The diagnosis is established by the combination of:

ECG DIAGNOSTIC CRITERIA (Atrial Flutter):

1. SAWTOOTH PATTERN (Flutter Waves):
- Characteristic negative deflections in inferior leads (II, III, aVF)
- Regular flutter waves at rate ~300/min (typical range 240-340/min, most commonly 300/min)
- No isoelectric baseline between flutter waves (continuous sawtooth appearance)
- Best visualised in leads II, III, aVF, V1

2. REGULAR NARROW COMPLEX TACHYCARDIA:
- QRS duration normal (90 ms, <120 ms)
- Regular ventricular rhythm (constant R-R intervals)
- Ventricular rate 150 bpm

3. 2:1 AV CONDUCTION:
- Atrial rate 300/min → Ventricular rate 150/min = 2:1 block (AV node conducts every second flutter wave)
- This is the MOST COMMON presentation of atrial flutter (60-70% present with 2:1 conduction)
- Mathematical rule: If regular narrow complex tachycardia at ~150 bpm → consider atrial flutter with 2:1 conduction until proven otherwise

4. NO DISCRETE P WAVES:
- Flutter waves replace normal P waves
- Distinguishes from sinus tachycardia (which has discrete upright P waves in lead II)

ATRIAL FLUTTER PATHOPHYSIOLOGY (Option B - CORRECT):

Atrial flutter is a macro-re-entrant atrial tachycardia, most commonly involving the cavotricuspid isthmus in the right atrium (typical flutter, 90% of cases). Re-entrant circuit produces organised atrial activation at ~300 bpm. AV node cannot conduct all impulses (protective decremental conduction), resulting in variable AV block:

- 2:1 block → HR 150 bpm (most common, 60-70% of cases)
- 3:1 block → HR 100 bpm (seen with rate-controlling medications)
- 4:1 block → HR 75 bpm (well-controlled)
- Variable block → Irregular ventricular rhythm (can mimic AF)

EPIDEMIOLOGY:
- Prevalence increases with age (0.1% at age 50 → 1% at age 80)
- Male predominance (2.5:1)
- Risk factors: Hypertension (this patient), structural heart disease, COPD, obesity, sleep apnoea, alcohol, thyrotoxicosis
- Often coexists with atrial fibrillation (50% of flutter patients have AF episodes)

CLINICAL PRESENTATION (matches this case):

- Palpitations ('rapid regular fluttering' - patient's description is classic)
- Dyspnoea on exertion (reduced cardiac output due to loss of atrial kick + rapid rate)
- Fatigue, dizziness (less common than AF)
- May be asymptomatic (incidental finding)
- Symptoms often better tolerated than AF (regular rhythm allows some cardiac compensation)

WHY OTHER OPTIONS ARE INCORRECT:

Option A (Atrial Fibrillation): AF produces IRREGULARLY IRREGULAR rhythm with fibrillatory waves (chaotic atrial activity 350-600/min), not regular rhythm. This patient has REGULAR rhythm at 150 bpm with organised flutter waves at 300/min. ECG would show: No P waves, irregular R-R intervals, fibrillatory baseline (best in V1). AF excluded by regular rhythm.

Option C (Sinus Tachycardia): Sinus tachycardia shows discrete upright P waves in lead II (one P wave before each QRS), rate 100-160 bpm. Gradual onset/offset related to physiological stress (fever, pain, hypovolaemia, anxiety). This patient has sawtooth flutter waves, not discrete P waves. Sinus tachycardia rarely exceeds 150 bpm in elderly at rest (maximum predicted HR = 220 - age = 152 bpm). No clear trigger for sinus tachycardia in this case.

Option D (AVNRT): Atrioventricular nodal re-entrant tachycardia presents with sudden-onset regular narrow complex tachycardia (140-220 bpm, most commonly 180 bpm), but NO flutter waves. P waves are either buried in QRS or appear as pseudo-R' waves in V1, pseudo-S waves in inferior leads (retrograde P waves). AVNRT typically presents in younger patients (20s-40s), sudden onset (seconds), responsive to vagal manoeuvres/adenosine. This patient is 68 years old with 3-day gradual onset - more consistent with flutter than AVNRT.

Option E (Multifocal Atrial Tachycardia - MAT): MAT shows IRREGULAR rhythm with at least 3 different P wave morphologies (different atrial foci), varying PR intervals, rate 100-150 bpm. Classic in COPD patients with respiratory failure (theophylline toxicity, hypoxia). ECG shows discrete P waves of varying morphology, not flutter waves. This patient has regular rhythm with sawtooth pattern - not MAT.

DIAGNOSTIC MANOEUVRES TO REVEAL FLUTTER WAVES:

If flutter waves not clearly visible on initial ECG (2:1 conduction can mask them):
1. Vagal manoeuvres (Valsalva, carotid massage): Transiently increase AV block (e.g., 2:1 → 4:1), slowing ventricular rate and revealing flutter waves
2. Adenosine 6 mg IV: Causes transient complete AV block (3-15 seconds), unmasks flutter waves (atrial rate continues at 300/min while ventricles pause). Diagnostic but doesn't terminate flutter.
3. Lewis lead ECG: Modified lead placement to enhance atrial activity

AUSTRALIAN MANAGEMENT (eTG Cardiovascular 2025):

ACUTE (this presentation):

1. RATE CONTROL (first-line if haemodynamically stable):
- Beta-blockers: Metoprolol 25-50 mg PO TDS or 5 mg IV (slow onset)
- Calcium channel blockers: Diltiazem 60 mg PO TDS or verapamil 40-80 mg PO TDS
- Digoxin 250-500 microgram IV (useful if heart failure present)
- Target: Ventricular rate <100 bpm at rest, <110 bpm with exertion

2. RHYTHM CONTROL (if symptomatic despite rate control):
- DC cardioversion: 50-100 joules biphasic (highly effective, >90% success)
- Chemical cardioversion: Ibutilide 1 mg IV over 10 min (50-70% success, risk of torsades 2-4%)
- Flecainide 300 mg PO (if no structural heart disease)
- Amiodarone 300 mg IV (if structural heart disease present)

3. ANTICOAGULATION ASSESSMENT:
- CHA2DS2-VASc score (same as AF): C-Congestive heart failure, H-Hypertension (1 point this patient), A-Age >75 (0), D-Diabetes (0), S-Stroke/TIA (2 points), V-Vascular disease (0), A-Age 65-74 (1 point this patient), S-Sex female (1 point this patient)
- Score = 3 → Anticoagulation recommended (apixaban 5 mg BD or rivaroxaban 20 mg daily preferred over warfarin)
- If duration >48 hours (this case: 3 days) → Either TOE to exclude thrombus before cardioversion OR anticoagulate 3 weeks before cardioversion + 4 weeks after

LONG-TERM (definitive):

1. CATHETER ABLATION (CURATIVE):
- Radiofrequency ablation of cavotricuspid isthmus (creates line of block)
- Success rate >95% for typical flutter
- First-line for recurrent symptomatic flutter (Class I recommendation ACC/AHA/ESC)
- Complication rate <1% (bleeding, tamponade, AV block rare)
- Single procedure, outpatient, local anaesthetic

2. ANTIARRHYTHMIC DRUGS (if ablation declined/contraindicated):
- Sotalol 80 mg BD (beta-blocker + Class III antiarrhythmic)
- Flecainide 100 mg BD (if no structural heart disease)
- Amiodarone 200 mg daily (if structural heart disease)
- Less effective than ablation, require lifelong therapy, side effects

THIS CASE MANAGEMENT:

1. Admit to monitored bed (telemetry ward)
2. Rate control: Metoprolol 50 mg PO TDS (patient already on ACE inhibitor, no contraindication to beta-blocker)
3. Anticoagulation: CHA2DS2-VASc score 3 → Start apixaban 5 mg BD (patient >60 kg, Cr <133 micromol/L)
4. If symptomatic despite rate control: DC cardioversion (require 3 weeks anticoagulation first OR TOE to exclude thrombus)
5. Cardiology referral for catheter ablation (curative, prevents recurrence)

RURAL CONTEXT (Young District Hospital):

- Rate control can be initiated in rural hospital
- DC cardioversion possible if equipment/trained staff available (check if cardiologist/anaesthetist on-site for sedation)
- Catheter ablation requires transfer to tertiary centre (Wagga Base Hospital electrophysiology or Sydney tertiary centres)
- TOE requires specialist (may need retrieval to Wagga/Sydney)
- Telehealth cardiology consultation recommended for management planning

SAFETY NETTING:

- If patient develops irregular rhythm: May indicate progression to AF (common), reassess anticoagulation
- If rate uncontrolled despite medications: Consider cardioversion or specialist review
- If patient becomes unstable (SBP <90 mmHg, chest pain, pulmonary oedema): Immediate cardioversion
- Educate: Palpitations may recur → Return if prolonged (>1 hour) or associated with chest pain/dyspnoea

MEDICOLEGAL:

Failing to recognise atrial flutter (mistaking for sinus tachycardia) and missing anticoagulation indication (CHA2DS2-VASc 3) would expose patient to stroke risk. Documentation should state: 'ECG shows atrial flutter with 2:1 conduction (flutter waves 300/min, ventricular rate 150/min). CHA2DS2-VASc score 3 - anticoagulation commenced as per Australian guidelines.'

REFERENCES:
- eTG Cardiovascular: Atrial flutter management (Therapeutic Guidelines Limited, 2025)
- National Heart Foundation of Australia: Atrial fibrillation and atrial flutter guidelines (2023)
- Cardiac Society of Australia and New Zealand: Anticoagulation in atrial arrhythmias (2024)
- Australian Resuscitation Council Guideline 11.6: Tachycardia algorithm (2024)
mcqs.summary: Atrial flutter: Regular narrow complex tachycardia with characteristic 'sawtooth' pattern (flutter waves) in inferior leads (II, III, aVF). Atrial rate typically 300/min, ventricular rate depends on AV conduction ratio. Most common presentation: 2:1 conduction (atrial 300 → ventricular 150 bpm). Rule: Regular narrow complex tachycardia at ~150 bpm → suspect flutter. Diagnosis confirmed by flutter waves (vagal manoeuvres/adenosine unmask if not visible). Management: (1) Rate control (beta-blockers, calcium channel blockers), (2) Anticoagulation per CHA2DS2-VASc score (same as AF), (3) Rhythm control (DC cardioversion 50-100J or chemical with ibutilide/flecainide), (4) DEFINITIVE: Catheter ablation of cavotricuspid isthmus (>95% cure rate, first-line for recurrent symptomatic flutter). If duration >48 hours: Anticoagulate 3 weeks before + 4 weeks after cardioversion OR TOE to exclude thrombus.

question.scenario: A 62-year-old man presents to cardiology outpatient clinic at Wagga Base Hospital (referred from Young District Hospital) for management of recurrent symptomatic atrial flutter. He has had 3 episodes in the past 6 months, each requiring Emergency Department attendance for rate control and cardioversion. Episodes last 6-24 hours, cause palpitations and dyspnoea on exertion. Past medical history: Hypertension (well-controlled on irbesartan 150 mg daily), hyperlipidaemia (atorvastatin 40 mg nocte). Transthoracic echocardiogram shows: Normal left ventricular systolic function (EF 60%), mild left atrial enlargement (LA volume index 32 mL/m²), no valvular disease. Currently in sinus rhythm on sotalol 80 mg BD (started after last episode 3 weeks ago). Patient reports sotalol causing fatigue and dizziness. He asks about long-term treatment options and whether there is a 'cure' for his flutter. CHA2DS2-VASc score = 3 (hypertension, age 65-74, male). On apixaban 5 mg BD for stroke prevention.
question.stem: What is the most appropriate long-term management strategy?

options.A: Continue sotalol 80 mg BD long-term for rhythm control
options.B: Switch to amiodarone 200 mg daily for more effective rhythm control
options.C: Switch to rate control strategy with metoprolol and accept permanent atrial flutter
options.D: Refer for catheter ablation of cavotricuspid isthmus
options.E: Increase sotalol dose to 160 mg BD for better arrhythmia suppression

mcqs.explanation:
CLINICAL REASONING:

This patient has recurrent symptomatic atrial flutter despite antiarrhythmic therapy (sotalol), with significant side effects (fatigue, dizziness). He has structurally normal heart (normal EF, no significant valvular disease) and is asking about curative options. This clinical scenario is the IDEAL indication for catheter ablation - the definitive treatment for typical atrial flutter.

CATHETER ABLATION FOR ATRIAL FLUTTER (Option D - CORRECT):

PROCEDURE:

Radiofrequency or cryoablation of the cavotricuspid isthmus (CTI) - the critical slow conduction zone in the typical flutter re-entrant circuit (right atrium, between inferior vena cava and tricuspid annulus). Creates complete bidirectional conduction block across isthmus, preventing re-entry.

Technique:
- Percutaneous approach via femoral vein (local anaesthetic, conscious sedation)
- Electrophysiology study to confirm typical flutter circuit
- Radiofrequency energy applied point-by-point across isthmus (or cryoablation -60°C)
- Bidirectional block confirmed by pacing manoeuvres
- Outpatient procedure, 1-2 hours duration, home same day or next day

SUCCESS RATES:

- Acute success (bidirectional block achieved): >95%
- Long-term success (freedom from flutter at 1 year): 85-95%
- Recurrence rate: 5-15% (usually due to gap in ablation line - can re-ablate)
- Single procedure success: 85%, repeat procedure if needed increases to >95%

COMPLICATIONS (low risk):

- Major complications: <1% (cardiac tamponade, vascular injury, stroke, AV block)
- Minor complications: 2-5% (groin haematoma, pericarditis)
- Mortality: <0.1%
- AV block risk <0.5% (CTI ablation distant from AV node, lower risk than AVNRT ablation)

GUIDELINES RECOMMENDATION:

ACC/AHA/ESC Guidelines (Class I, Level of Evidence A):
- Catheter ablation is FIRST-LINE therapy for recurrent symptomatic atrial flutter
- Recommended over long-term antiarrhythmic drugs due to:
  * Higher success rate (>90% vs 50-60% with drugs)
  * Curative (no need for lifelong medications)
  * Better quality of life (no drug side effects)
  * Cost-effective (single procedure vs lifelong drug costs + ED visits)

ADVANTAGES OVER MEDICAL THERAPY:

1. CURATIVE: Eliminates substrate for flutter (vs suppressive therapy with drugs)
2. HIGH SUCCESS RATE: 90-95% freedom from flutter (vs 50-60% with antiarrhythmics)
3. AVOIDS DRUG SIDE EFFECTS:
   - Sotalol: Fatigue, dizziness, bradycardia, bronchospasm, torsades de pointes (2-3%)
   - Amiodarone: Thyroid dysfunction (15%), pulmonary fibrosis (5%), hepatotoxicity, corneal deposits
   - Flecainide: Atrial fibrillation conversion (pro-arrhythmic), contraindicated in structural heart disease
4. SINGLE PROCEDURE: No lifelong medication adherence required
5. COST-EFFECTIVE: Ablation cost offset by reduced ED visits, hospitalisations, drug costs
6. QUALITY OF LIFE: Studies show significant improvement post-ablation vs medical therapy

PATIENT SELECTION (this patient is IDEAL candidate):

Ideal:
- Recurrent symptomatic flutter (this patient: 3 episodes in 6 months)
- Failed or intolerant to antiarrhythmic drugs (this patient: sotalol causing fatigue/dizziness)
- Structurally normal heart (this patient: EF 60%, no significant valvular disease)
- Typical flutter (CTI-dependent, >90% of cases)
- Patient preference for cure over lifelong medications (this patient asking about 'cure')

Less ideal (but still consider):
- Atypical flutter (non-CTI dependent) - success rates lower (70-80%)
- Severe structural heart disease (risk assessment needed)
- Concurrent atrial fibrillation (50% of flutter patients develop AF post-ablation - may need AF ablation later)

ANTICOAGULATION POST-ABLATION:

IMPORTANT: Even if flutter cured, this patient MUST continue anticoagulation (apixaban) because:
1. CHA2DS2-VASc score 3 → ongoing stroke risk regardless of rhythm
2. 50% of flutter patients develop atrial fibrillation (shared risk factors: HTN, LA enlargement)
3. Australian/international guidelines: Continue anticoagulation per CHA2DS2-VASc score even after successful ablation

WHY OTHER OPTIONS ARE SUBOPTIMAL:

Option A (Continue sotalol): Patient is symptomatic on sotalol (fatigue, dizziness) and has had recurrent flutter despite therapy (3 episodes in 6 months). Continuing same medication unlikely to prevent recurrences and patient quality of life poor. Sotalol also carries 2-3% risk of torsades de pointes (polymorphic VT). Suboptimal when curative option (ablation) available.

Option B (Switch to amiodarone): Amiodarone more effective than sotalol for rhythm control (70% vs 60% success) but has significant long-term toxicity:
- Thyroid dysfunction: 15-20% (hyper or hypothyroidism) - requires 6-monthly TFTs
- Pulmonary fibrosis: 5-10% - potentially fatal, requires baseline + annual CXR/PFTs
- Hepatotoxicity: 15% - requires 6-monthly LFTs
- Corneal deposits: 90% (usually asymptomatic but can cause halos/glare)
- Skin photosensitivity, blue-grey skin discolouration
- Drug interactions (warfarin, digoxin, statins)
